title: Church of God and those who call on the Name (1 Cor 1:2–10)
english: Fragments from the commentaries on the First Letter to the Corinthians. On 1 Corinthians 1:2: “to the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints, together with all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, theirs and ours.” Origen says: if everyone were already the church, what need would there still be to add “together with all who call upon”? And if all alike were calling upon the Name, what need would there be for the letter not to be written only to all who call upon it, but beyond them also to the church of God? We have already shown that only those who deserve praise ought to be styled “church,” while those who deserve blame are not yet apostates—they are still wrestling with sin—but are still calling upon him, and are not yet the church itself. So let us hurry on from mere calling upon him to rising up into the church that is spotless and without blemish.

On 1 Corinthians 1:4–10: “I thank my God always concerning you for the grace of God given you in Christ Jesus, that in everything you were enriched in him, in every word and all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed among you, so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will also confirm you to the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord. I appeal to you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be fitted together in the same mind and the same judgment.” Origen says: neither do these praises suit sinners, nor do those rebukes suit the righteous alone—I mean the words “I appeal to you, brothers… that you all say the same things and that there be no divisions among you,” and whatever is like them. So the church was mixed, if one may even call “church” this whole blend of just and unjust. Still, those who were gathering were mixed; therefore, when the apostle was about to convict the gathering for sins done with wickedness, he first, of necessity, offers praise for those who come together well upon the same thing.

“I thank my God always”: it is right to give thanks over the praiseworthy things he names, and not sometimes to thank and sometimes not, but always to thank. If I see someone sometimes doing well and sometimes sinning, I do not thank God concerning him always, but when he does well—and so also concerning myself. In whom, then, does the thanksgiving Paul offer find its ground? In his own hearers, of whom he has become a father according to God. Just as a father gives thanks over sons when they are healthy and when they prosper, so too, whenever a teacher sees his hearers boiling with the Spirit, rich in word and wisdom, worthy of praise, he thanks God always concerning them. Let us look, then, at the grace of those praised in Corinth, so that we may be eager for it.

“That in everything you were enriched in him.” Blessed are those who are rich in everything and lack nothing that belongs to God, but practice every virtue and enjoy his gifts freely and richly—in every word and in all knowledge—so that they are at a loss over no Scripture, but seek and find everywhere; and when a text must be explained they can use every kind of discourse, both the so called continuous exposition and question and answer, and are ready to speak against every heresy, to stand with the dogma of the truth, and to fulfill what the apostle said: “Always ready to make a defense to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you.” So also “in all knowledge”: not only according to the Scriptures, but so that one may say, “For he himself gave me unfailing knowledge of the things that are,” and what follows from that. For knowledge shows knowing alone, while word also interprets what is known. “Just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed”

title: Christ’s testimony confirmed; gifts; faithful God; baptism and the cross (1 Cor 1:6–18)
english: among you. Christ is, if I may put it this way, the chief martyr; and though there are many witnesses to Christ through their death, he is the ruler of the martyrs. This testimony of Christ is firm in some, and in others it is not firm but shaken. For if faith about the testimony is such that from a true disposition one can say, “I am persuaded that neither death nor life” and what follows “will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord,” then the testimony is firm in such a person; but if we are not like that, and are shaken by what happens, the testimony of Christ has not yet been confirmed in us. And again we may take the saying another way: every Scripture that bears witness about Christ is a testimony of Christ; so it is good to be confirmed also in the testimony of Christ that comes from the Scriptures. And otherwise: look at the testimony of Christ—signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will also bore witness with him; and the testimony of Christ is firm in the saints.

“So that you are not lacking in any gift”: as there are many gifts, he will discuss them also later in the letter. “Awaiting the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ”: the righteous person does not have his hopes in this age, but while suffering and facing danger he awaits the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, what Christ Jesus reveals. “Who will also confirm you to the end”: who confirms? Christ Jesus, the Word, Wisdom; and the testimony that is being confirmed is not for a few days, but to the end. “Blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ”: until we arrive there, we do not yet have blamelessness; for we do not know what the coming day will bring forth, and even if someone seems to have blamelessness for the present, it is in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

On 1 Corinthians 1:9: “God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.” Origen: keep believing him always; for you were called so that we might simply be under Jesus. Great is what God grants the saints: we were called into fellowship with his Son; therefore heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. On 1 Corinthians 1:10: “and that there be no divisions among you.” Origen: the one who agrees in everything with the right word and the church’s dogma concerning Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and further concerning the economy that touches us, concerning resurrection and judgment, and who also follows the church’s canons, is not in a schism.

On 1 Corinthians 1:14, 17: “I thank God that I baptized none of you… for Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, not in wisdom of word, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied.” Origen: preaching the gospel is greater than baptizing; and because Paul knew that some were set apart for baptizing, he thanks God for having a better lot than baptizing. In Acts the apostles’ works appear: Philip baptized, but Philip did not minister the Spirit to the baptized; rather Peter laid hands on those Philip baptized, and the Spirit came upon them. Philip baptized with water those being born again of water and Holy Spirit, and Peter with the Spirit. Origen again: there is need not so much of word as of power; therefore it is written, “The Lord will give a word to those who preach good news with great power,” the King of the powers of the Beloved. So Christ sent me not to baptize but to preach the gospel, not in wisdom of word, not in clarity of diction; for if I do that and want to hand on the word that way, the power of Christ does not reach the soul of the hearers, and I empty and tear down the grace of the power.

On 1 Corinthians 1:18: “For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” Origen: the name of the cross seems a scandal; but if someone lends his ears to the word of God and to grace, he will see that this too is a great mystery. Even the pagans have handed down that often, when great plagues or floods or droughts came, these ceased when a person gave himself up for the common good. Why then is it surprising if, when the whole world was sick with error, one had to die for the true plague—to destroy the plague of ignorance and darkness and ruin? And who was able to take this on? Not a prophet, not an apostle, nor any other righteous person; but a divine power had to come down from heaven

title: Cross as trophy; true folly and wisdom; Christ crucified (1 Cor 1:18–31)
english: able to take on dying for all, with a kind of public display, so that through that death a trophy might be raised against the devil. For those who triumph in the world are accustomed to set up trophies against the conquered in the manner of a cross. So the cross of Christ is a trophy against Satan; therefore he says, “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross”—for the one who has come to know what the power of the cross is: that I was freed from evils through that One who died to rescue me from death—“except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.” It is a great good that the world has been crucified to me; through what did this good come to me? Through the cross of Christ. It is a great good for me to be crucified to the world; for if I died to the world, I have been crucified to the world with Christ; but if I live in sins, I have not yet been counted worthy of the good that belongs to the cross. At the same time let us also prepare for trials and for martyrdoms, knowing that whoever denies him has no salvation.

On 1 Corinthians 1:19–21: “For it is written, ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will set aside.’ Where is the wise? Where the scribe? Where the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom, God was pleased through the folly of the preaching to save those who believe.” Origen: it is not the same to be wise and to be wise in this age; for without such an addition the word covers true wisdom. You will understand folly likewise: it is not the same to be a fool and to be a fool in this age; for without the addition “in this age” one is truly a fool. We who believe the words of wisdom are therefore commanded to become fools in this age; for so we seem to people when we believe in Christ Jesus crucified, and believe the resurrection of bodies, and believe that we shall live—not only that those now on earth will later be in the heavens, but that if we sin we shall be handed over to eternal fire. Such we seem to people…

On 1 Corinthians 1:23–31: “but we preach Christ crucified, a scandal to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God… For consider your calling, brothers, that not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many of noble birth; but God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong, and God chose the of low birth of the world and the despised, and the things that are not, to abolish the things that are, so that no flesh may boast before God. And from him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.’” Origen: we received power from believing in Jesus Christ crucified; and as far as we fall short in that faith, so far we fall short in the power of having in ourselves the things that come from God. And if you want to understand “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and set aside the discernment of the discerning,” picture for me someone very formidable in heretical arguments—say Marcion or Basilides—who seeks with such force for the heretical case that not just anyone can stand against him; then picture someone competent according to the truth, whom God also made competent as a minister of a new covenant, showing all those things to be folly on which the deceived man relied. So he destroys their wisdom—not that of the truly wise, Isaiah, Jeremiah, or Solomon; he destroys seeming wisdom, not the true. And how “in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom”? The wisdom of God is in law and prophets; the world did not know Christ preached in law and prophets. Therefore at the end of the ages he sent Jesus Christ to be crucified for the human race, so that by the folly of the preaching those who believed in Jesus Christ crucified might believe. And he added “according to the flesh” to “not many wise,” knowing there are differences among the wise: some wise according to flesh, some according to spirit; and wise according to flesh are those who have practiced only little phrases and dress up whatever is not truth as if it were truth

title: Wise according to flesh and powerful according to Spirit; things that are not; foundation of faith (1 Cor 1:26–2:8)
english: —what is not truth. Yet even so he did not shut the wise according to flesh out of the faith; for he did not say “No one wise according to the flesh comes to the word,” but that they are exceedingly few. Powerful according to the flesh are those who hold the offices; according to the Spirit you will understand if you see how the Savior was not powerful according to the flesh—he was handed over and crucified from weakness—yet was powerful according to the Spirit, healing every disease and every illness in the people. So look at the apostles: how they were powerful according to the Spirit. One is powerful according to the Spirit also who lives according to the Spirit and by the Spirit puts to death the deeds of the body. Likewise with the of noble birth: of noble birth according to the flesh are those from rich and famous fathers; according to the Spirit the of noble birth are the sons of God, of whom it is written, “As many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God.” Whom then did God choose? Not simply the foolish, but with the addition “of the world”: we who believe are fools as far as the world is concerned. So they laugh and call us fools: “Christians say there is a resurrection of the dead, and that we live after death, and that Jesus whom the Jews crucified was born of a virgin,” and such things. Let them laugh and call us fools; for the soulish person does not receive the things of the Spirit—they are folly to him. So God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise—not simply the wise, but, by common construction, of the world: God chose the world’s foolish to shame the world’s wise; for truly the world’s wise are put to shame when they worship idols while the unlettered and simple die rather than commit idolatry.

“And God chose the of low birth of the world and the despised”—again with the addition “of the world.” For what is nobler than a soul that leaves the idols and says, “Our fathers acquired false idols, and there is none among them who brings rain”? So God chose the of low birth of the world but of noble birth of God; only let us succeed so that we are not despised before God, of whom it is written that the one who does evil is despised before him. “And the things that are not, to abolish the things that are”: he named “things that are not” the foolish, weak, of low birth, and despised of the world; “things that are,” the of noble birth of the world—for in the world they are somebody, and we are not, worn down by all and despised. Now God chose the things that are not to abolish the things that are, so that no flesh may boast and say, “I was chosen because I am of noble birth.” “And from him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption”: for this reason Christ is all these for us, so that what is written may come to pass—“Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” For if the one who boasts in wisdom ought to boast, and Christ is the wisdom, clearly the one who boasts in Christ boasts; and likewise for the rest—I mean sanctification and righteousness.

On 1 Corinthians 2:4–7: “and my word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in demonstration of Spirit and power, so that your faith might not be in human wisdom but in the power of God. Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect—wisdom not of this age nor of the rulers of this age who are being abolished. But we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predestined before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.” Origen: lest someone say, “Then, since he brought the proofs of faith in power and in Spirit, he had no wisdom at all, but the mystery of piety is only to believe, and there is no promise of wisdom in it,” he adds, “Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect—wisdom not of this age nor of the rulers of this age who are being abolished.” For it is one thing to lead people into the faith, and another to unveil the wisdom of God. So we unfold God’s wisdom not to those being introduced, nor to beginners, nor to those who have not yet given proof of a sound life; but when someone, having exercised the senses as one ought toward distinguishing good and evil, becomes fit also to hear wisdom, then we speak wisdom among the perfect—and I mean wisdom not

title: Wisdom in a mystery; depths of God; taught by the Spirit words (1 Cor 2:6–15)
english: of this age, nor anything like the wisdom of the rulers of this age. At the same time he has made clear that the lessons circulating among others are not, in their origin, of humans but of invisible powers that are being abolished. And I would say that the poetic wisdom is of this age, and perhaps rhetoric too; and so is the wisdom that claims to speak about heaven and earth and the administration of the whole. So if we speak wisdom and say it among the perfect, we do not mean the wisdom of this age; for it is not through poems or through any such art. Origen: but we speak wisdom in a mystery—things unknown to the rulers of this age who work the wisdom of the wise of this world; and thus they did not know: they plotted against our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ and crucified him; for if they had known they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. Therefore wisdom must also be sought in the word—but after faith, after the way of life, according to what is written: “Desire wisdom; keep the commandments.”

On 1 Corinthians 2:9–11: “But as it is written, ‘What eye has not seen and ear has not heard and has not risen upon a human heart—what God prepared for those who love him.’ But to us God revealed them through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. For who among humans knows the things of a human except the spirit of the human that is in him? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.” Origen: Scripture knows a difference between those who love God and those who fear God, and knows that those who love far surpass those who fear. Some things have been prepared also for those who fear; yet he prepared something greater for those who love than what was prepared for those who fear. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. There is a Spirit that can search everything; the human soul cannot search everything, but a better Spirit had to come to be in us, so that when that Spirit is in us searching everything—even the depths of God—and is mingled with us, we may search together with it everything and the depths of God.

On 1 Corinthians 2:12–15: “Now we have not received the spirit of the world but the Spirit that is from God, so that we may know the things freely given us by God; which things we also speak not in words taught by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the soulish person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he cannot know them because they are spiritually examined. The spiritual person examines all things, yet he himself is examined by no one.” Origen: let us understand the things freely given us by God; for if the Spirit from God that teaches us is not in us, we cannot say that we know the things freely given us by God—for no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. “Which things we also speak,” he says, “not in words taught by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit,” and what follows. All the wisdoms of this world are words taught by humans, which one learns in each of the rational arts; but they do not teach the things taught by the Spirit; and you would not say that the teacher, taught by the Spirit about what he says, taught them. For the Spirit present in the one who seeks and searches the truth shines in, and so always, by the renewal of the mind, he finds what he has not learned from humans. title: Comparing spiritual with spiritual; soulish and spiritual; milk and solid food (1 Cor 2:13–3:2)
english: Spirit is to be understood from the apostolic words: “comparing spiritual things with spiritual”—by examining this wording with that wording and gathering like with like, the mind of Scripture is uncovered as it were. In this way I understand the things of God and become taught by the Spirit: not only by having learned the things of the Spirit that moved Isaiah, but also by having the same Spirit that shut and sealed Isaiah’s words; for unless the Spirit opens the prophets’ words, what is shut cannot be opened. And since he said these things, he necessarily adds that there are some people who do not receive the things of the Spirit of God—not because of nature, as the heterodox suppose, but because they have not prepared themselves. For the soulish person does not receive the things of the Spirit—he was soulish; but when he inclined toward piety and received the Spirit, he became spiritual. And the soulish cannot know that he is examined spiritually; therefore he does not know, about what he hears, that it is examined spiritually; and when the power is tested it convicts the fool—as when I speak taught by the Spirit and speak with power, and the hearer testing the power thinks otherwise and does not assent: the power being tested convicts the fool. And it is not so much that he has rejected what is said as that what is said has rejected him; for “wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil, nor dwell in a body in debt to sin.” “The spiritual person examines all things, yet he himself is examined by no one.” The one who no longer walks according to flesh but according to Spirit, and always by care grows it and kindles more the gift of God, prepares for himself to become spiritual; and having become so he is able to examine all things—the Greeks’, the barbarians’, the wise’, the senseless’; and no one can examine him because of the greatness of his understanding and of his reasonings. And if you want to recognize the spiritual person, “by their fruits you will know them.” What then are the fruits of the Spirit by which one must know who is spiritual? Hear the apostle: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self control”; where these are, there is the Spirit, and that one is spiritual; and where any of these is missing, that one is not yet spiritual.

On 1 Corinthians 3:1–3a: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual people but as to fleshly, as to infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able; but neither are you able even now.” Origen: of hearers some are perfect—the spiritual, of whom we were also speaking earlier; and those who are not spiritual yet believe in Christ are, as the apostle says, infants in Christ and fleshly in Christ—for I hear “in Christ” as common to both. So those not yet more perfect and not yet exercised in the sacred Scriptures need lesser lessons, which the apostle named milk: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able, but neither are you able even now.” And I think there is a scale among spiritual foods: milk, food, true food, solid food, flesh of the Word, and spiritual vegetable. And I dare to say this persuaded by the Scriptures; for he did not say every spiritual food is true food when he says, “My flesh is true food.” What then is not solid food? The more ethical teachings and whatever among ethical matters is weaker—said by way of concession, not by command, stewarded because of the hearers’ weakness. But whatever more perfect teaching among ethical matters belongs to eager and hardworking hearers—these I would call solid food among ethical teachings: teaching about perfect chastity, about virginity or temperance, about martyrdom; these are solid food. And solid food in mystical matters is teaching about Father and Son. So also the law sometimes hands on solid food, sometimes lesser. For example we come to the word about the snakes that killed the sons of Israel because of murmuring: if we read more simply, we say, “Let us not murmur, as some of them murmured and were destroyed by the snakes.” But if the hearer can hear a mystical word, we say who the snakes are and who the snake hung upon the wood, and how one is saved by looking to that snake—and so with each spiritual Scripture. title: Infants’ milk; jealousy and parties; planting and watering (1 Cor 3:2–8)
english: letter when he says, “Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk”; and in Hebrews also, “You have become ones who need milk and not solid food; for everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant; but solid food is for the perfect, who because of habit have their senses exercised toward distinguishing good and evil.”

On 1 Corinthians 3:3–5: “For where there is jealousy and strife and divisions among you, are you not fleshly and walking according to a human? For whenever someone says, ‘I am of Paul,’ and another, ‘I am of Apollos,’ are you not humans?” Origen: among human sins the lesser ones are jealousy and strife. If someone is in fornication, such a person is no longer fleshly but worse than fleshly. What then would such a one be? Let us see. I think there is a difference between fleshly and earthy: “As we bore the image of the earthy,” he says, “let us also bear the image of the heavenly.” So if you sin unto death, you are not fleshly but earthy; but if you sin, yet not unto death, you are not wholly earthy nor fallen away from the grace of Christ, but then you are fleshly. And of our walks, one is according to a human, another according to God. If we walk as most humans do, we walk according to a human; but if according to “Let your light shine before humans,” we differ from the many and do not walk according to a human. So the life is clear to the one who can see what is according to a human and what according to God. For whenever someone says, “I am of Paul,” “I am of Apollos,” “I am of Cephas”—let us also attend to these. We shall see that sometimes we are not even humans but worse than humans. For the one who then said “I am of Apollos” was speaking of a learned and holy and blessed man; the one who said “I am of Paul,” of a sacred and blessed apostle. But sometimes leanings arise not like the leaning toward Paul or Apollos, but someone leans toward a sinner and sometimes toward a heterodox person. So if those are humans and walk according to flesh who say “I am of Apollos” and “I of Paul,” whenever you say you belong to someone lesser, clearly you are no longer even a human but worse than human; and perhaps it will be said to you, “Brood of vipers.”

On 1 Corinthians 3:6–8: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth; so neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth… and each will receive his own wage according to his own labor.” Origen: if Paul planted, he planted together with God who plants first of all; if Apollos watered, he watered together with Christ who waters first of all; for God plants—therefore it is written, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted,” and again, “My Father is the farmer.” So let us bear fruit lest we be cut down like the barren fig tree. For every tree not producing good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Let us take care that it not be said of us, “I waited for it to produce grapes, and it produced thorns.” For if he says these things about us, he will also say what follows: “And now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will remove its hedge and it shall be for plunder, and I will tear down its wall and it shall be for trampling.”

On 1 Corinthians 3:9–15: “For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building. According to the grace of God given me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and another builds upon it. 1 Cor. 3:16–20: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone ruins God’s temple, God will ruin him; for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple. Let no one deceive himself. For it is written, ‘He catches the wise in their craftiness,’ and again, ‘The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.’”

Origen says: If you want to learn what the true temple of God is, seek living stones, cleanly quarried, set in place by the Word, standing four-square, with nothing unstable or rolling. For even if holy stones roll on the earth, the stonecutters do not let them keep rolling to the end. So you, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

And with the Apostle it is said that all of us are one temple, each of us a stone of the temple. So he speaks in Ephesians: “So then you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow-citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, in whom you also are being built together into a dwelling of God in the Spirit.”

So no stone must be ill-fitted to the building. For if two of you agree on earth about any matter they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven—how much more, then, if all the stones agree in one harmony and all share one heart and one soul, will their prayer be able and strong? It is good, then, that we all say the same thing, that we may be fitted together in the same mind and the same judgment; for so you are a building fitted together into a holy temple in the Lord.

And in another sense each of us can be a temple by himself. For if a temple is what has God’s glory, everyone who has God’s glory in himself is in that respect God’s temple. One has more glory or less who makes the name of the Father in heaven glorified by his deeds; therefore it is written, “Those who glorify me I will glorify.” Then we will most of all be God’s temple if we prepare ourselves to receive the Spirit of God. Yet no one who has a spirit of some sin can be God’s temple, because the Spirit of God alone dwells where he judges it right to dwell.

“If anyone ruins God’s temple, God will ruin him.” As far as each person can, even if he is a stone, he ruins God’s temple when he sins; and anyone who puts a stumbling-block before the church also ruins God’s temple. Still more properly the one who fornicates ruins God’s temple, since your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, which you have from God. So the pure person is called uncorrupted, and the one who is no longer a virgin is called corrupted—as if this deed alone were the corrupting. If, then, this is a work of corruption, let us guard against it above all; for the Lord also, with all who love God, is in incorruption.

And again: “The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.” It is no wonder if the Lord, by himself, knows that the reasonings of the wise are futile. But I want the Lord, come to be in me, to know that the reasonings of the wise are futile. For if Christ comes to be in me, he can set beside me how the reasonings of this world’s wise are futile, and how God’s wisdom alone shines, conquering and trampling every seeming wisdom.

title: Unit 3 rem mid
english: of God. He administers the mysteries of God, for example, toward Luke so that he may be able to write the Gospel, and toward Timothy so that he may begin to be able to manage those in Ephesus who have received more—and to steward the mysteries of God. I even dare to say that in Corinth he became a servant of Christ, but in Ephesus a steward of God’s mysteries.

Having learned from the Savior’s words—“Who then is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord will set over his household to give the food allowance in season to his fellow servants?”—Paul says, “Moreover, it is required in stewards that one be found faithful.” For it is not enough to have come to know, nor should the one who knows speak at random; rather, understanding that one must give the food allowance in season to his fellow servants, he must see which of the fellow servants ought to receive a larger measure of God’s mysteries, or a smaller, and when. For if he administers the stewardship well and blamelessly, what promise does he have? “Over all his goods,” he says, “the master of the house will set him.” And if Paul fears and says these things about himself and about Cephas and Apollos, how much more must the stewards among us fear that they may be found faithful stewards.

Then about himself he says, “But with me it is a very small thing that I should be examined by you or by a human day.” Those in Corinth examined as far as they could—not truly examining. For examining would be saying that Paul is better than Cephas and Apollos, and another’s examining would be saying that Peter far surpasses Paul; for in the Gospel Paul is not called an apostle. So Paul says that with him it is a very small thing to be examined by you. He was conscious in himself of the finest things, and that he did not fall under the Corinthians as people able to examine him; for “the spiritual person examines all things, yet he himself is examined by no one”—as elsewhere he says, “I have become a fool; you compelled me.” Something of that kind he means here too.

There is a human day, and there is a divine day, about which countless things are written, including “Behold, the day of the Lord comes.” So my examination, he says, cannot take place in a human day; for a human day cannot contain my examination. If I am going to be examined, I will be examined in the day of the Lord.

Then, more paradoxically conscious of himself, he says, “But I do not even examine myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself.” Here the Apostle’s conscience appears greatly purified—so much so that he dared to write not only to those then living, but so that generations until the end may also read what is said. True, then, is Paul when he says, “Become imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.” How Paul imitated Christ, hear: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me”; and Paul says, “I am not aware of anything against myself.” And he did not say, “I am not aware of any worthless deed against myself.” For if he had said that, we could say he is cleansed in works but not yet in words; or again, cleansed in these, while his heart still sinned. Now he seems to know in himself an excess of purity—not earlier when he persecuted, or when he came to the faith, but now when he was saying these things.

Then, lest he seem to have spoken above a human being, he adds and says, “But I am not thereby justified. For I,” he says, “am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby justified.” For it is possible that I know nothing against myself, and yet some sin of mine escapes me. For many such things happen in human nature that one sins not according to reason, not with grasping or assent, not with seeing that we have sinned. So that one who in all things is aware of nothing against himself says, “But I am not thereby justified; it is the Lord who examines me.”

As one who has passed beyond the examination of angels and of the other powers, he says this: “Until the Lord comes.” Since judgment lies ahead—and that of the Lord alone is true, who knows how to weigh thoughts and set words in a balance and search out all deeds and render to each of us what is due—therefore even if we condemn someone, let us not pass final sentence. For we do not know by what measure he sinned, nor with what disposition he sinned, nor whether he has good counterweights to his sin. If we become careful, we will not judge anything before the time, but will refer everything to the judgment of God through our Savior Jesus Christ.
Here it is said, “Do not judge anything before the time,” and what follows; but in another place in the letter: “Do you not judge those who are inside? But those outside God judges.”

title: Fragmenta ex commentariis in epistulam i ad Corinthios Unit 4 opening
english: They promise traditions and say, “These are beyond what is written; for our Savior handed these to the apostles in secret, and the apostles to so-and-so or so-and-so.” And thus through this myth-making they deceive the hearts of the simple. But the rest say, “It is written, ‘Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the beam in your own?’ and ‘Do not judge, that you may not be judged.’” For if we are one and bound to one another, we must not rise against one another. For “the one who humbles himself will be exalted,” and “the one who wants to be first among you must be last of all,” and “each should remain in that in which he was called.”

These and such things are written, so that none may be puffed up for the one against the other. For those who divided themselves—some wanting to be called of this one, some of that—fought one another, each eager to set their own teachers above the others, and then against the teachers themselves. “For who distinguishes you? Who appointed you of a party? Why are you not called teacher of all alike? What do you have that you did not receive? On what do you think highly? On fluency of speech? But God has granted you this. On knowledge? This too is a divine gift. On wonder-works? This also is the Spirit’s working. And if you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” No one thinks highly over another’s deposits; he watches over them to keep them for the one who gave them.

One must gather from the Scriptures what “distinguish” means, so that we may apply it to what is now said. “God stands in the assembly of gods; in the midst he distinguishes gods.” Here distinguishing appears as God’s work. Judging being something else—what falls on those worthy of judgment—it is good to be found a god in the assembly of gods, so that one is no longer judged but distinguished, and as it were entrusted one rank of those entrusted to the gods in assembly. But also in “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others distinguish,” distinguishing there seems taken as articulating—clarify what is said, distinguish it, and understand it. And in “The one who distinguishes, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith,” the one distinguishing appears spoken of for blame. And again: “Welcome one another, not distinguishing with reasonings when you sin.” So from Scripture the word is sometimes set on the better and sometimes on the opposite.

Here, then, “distinguish” means: no one among those in Corinth distinguishes you or judges you; but you distinguish a steward of God’s mysteries and say, “I am of Paul,” and claim, “I of Cephas,” or say, “I am of Apollos.” Distinguishing the apostles is God’s work, not yours. Just as you must not judge, you must not distinguish the servants of the gospel. For in the distinction by which you distinguish the apostles, you distinguish and separate yourself, sinning. For Christ came to unite what had been distinguished, so that we would no longer be divided. If we are perfected so that the flesh no longer desires against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh—by putting to death the members that are on the earth—we will no longer be in distinction but as it were in mixture and in our gathering to the same. Let it also be understood more simply of various schisms.

1 Cor. 4:9–10: “For I think God has exhibited us apostles last, as sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world and to angels and to human beings. In Corinth, then, someone contracted an unlawful marriage; he took his stepmother. title: Incorruption, mutual debt, and agreed continence (1 Cor 6–7)
english: someone destroys of the Spirit; but toward the Father, when I destroy the temple of God. In addition, then, however many sins we commit—even if we commit murders—yet if we remain uncorrupted and have not tasted the corruption that belongs to intercourse, we are not said to have been corrupted by having murdered. But since both incorruption and corruption concern the nature that is without taste of sexual pleasure—for we say “the virgin was corrupted,” and again “the young man is uncorrupted,” or “he was corrupted”—every sin that a person commits is outside the body (1 Corinthians 6:18). Since therefore a ransom was given for you, the blood of Christ, and he took you from the authority of the devil, glorify God in your body, that your body may become worthy of blessedness as of those who have loved incorruption, as also the apostle says: the grace of God be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption (Ephesians 6:24).

Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. But because of the cases of sexual immorality, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband give to the wife her due, and likewise also the wife to the husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does (1 Corinthians 7:1–4).

People who sin, speaking generally, sin in two ways: by falling short of the commandments or by going beyond them. For when we do not live from knowledge and, not knowing the measures of righteousness, we slip, and sometimes by overshooting the rule in the fancy of doing something better we fall away from what is set before us. The proper weight, then—which is neither large nor small but commensurate—is to know how one ought to live. You have been bound with a wife: you make one large weight; you do not care for the wife but say: I am able to practice continence and live more purely. But see that your wife is being destroyed, unable to bear your purity, for whom Christ died. Something of this sort happened in Corinth, and there was disorder in the households of the brothers, husbands in one place and wives in another trying to practice continence and rising up against one another. So those in Corinth wrote a letter to the apostle about this, and to that letter the apostle writes back what has been written above. He neither stretched the word about chastity so as to abolish the word about marriage, nor, preferring marriage, abolished the word about virginity, as a good steward; but throughout the whole discourse he somehow keeps his wish and exhorts to purity; and having conceded condescension, he again exhorts to practice chastity; and having exhorted to practice chastity, he again brings them to the need to condescend to the weakness of the weaker. He began not from the lesser things—for that would not have been fitting—but from the more perfect matters, saying: Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me, it is good for a man not to touch a woman—as if: I praise you for having wished to live chastely, those who withdrew from mixture with the wife; but reckon not only your own interest but also the wife’s. For love does not seek its own (1 Corinthians 13:5). Therefore because of the cases of sexual immorality let each have his own wife, and each her own husband. Not because of his own fornication should the stronger keep his own wife, but lest somehow the wife fornicate because of the husband’s continence, and the husband because of the wife’s. For it is more choiceworthy that the two be saved while found in the works of marriage than that on the pretext of the one the other fall from the hope that is in Christ. For how will he also be saved who is liable for the death of the wife? The husband’s solemnity is not pure, then, when the exercise does not arise from the wife’s agreement for both to have leisure for prayers according to God.

title: Mutual authority, seasonal abstinence, and marriage as gift (1 Cor 7)
english: to heal human weakness and to arrange the matters in those places most becomingly; therefore he said a due is owed from the husband and to the husband from the wife. Then, lest he shame those in marriage as being slaves of one another who must not come to the exercise of purity without agreement, he says: The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife. The husband therefore has authority over the wife’s body, and having authority, if he wishes, let him not use the authority; “but we did not use this right,” says the apostle, teaching this, I think, when he says: Do we not have a right to take along a sister as wife, as also the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? (1 Corinthians 9:5). Does the wife then have authority over the husband’s body and is she unable not to use the authority? The word “likewise” set twice gives us to understand that the husband must not think that in the matters of marriage he excels the wife; there is likeness and equality for those married toward one another.

Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may have leisure for prayer, and be together again (1 Corinthians 7:5). You both ought to know that prayer from a man’s and a woman’s purity is not the same as prayer from intercourse. For if Greeks sometimes practice chastity before idols, how much more you who pray to the God of all? It is good, then, to condescend because of weakness, and to hold back because of prayers. Moses also purifies the people and says for three days not to approach a woman, that by having purified beforehand they may become hearers of God (Exodus 19:15). And in the Kingdoms, when Abathar or Ahimelech the priest wishes to set holy bread before David fleeing Saul’s plot, what does he say except: If the young men are clean from a woman?—not from a strange woman but from a wife (1 Samuel 21:4–5). Then, that someone may receive the bread of the Presence, he ought to be clean from a woman; but that he may receive the greater breads than the Presence, over which the name of God and of Christ and of the Holy Spirit has been invoked, how much more ought someone to be cleaner, that he may truly receive the breads unto salvation and not unto judgment?

Many think “deprive” is said only of gold or silver or something of that sort; but the apostle clearly named deprivation also concerning those in marriages who practice chastity unseasonably and without agreement. Once for all, simply, the one who does not render what is owed deprives the one to whom he owes by not rendering the due. Sometimes a person is shut in so that he cannot render two dues at once; therefore it is written that he may render the necessary due. What I mean will be clear thus: it is not possible both to render prayers to God as one ought and for the married man to render the due to the wife; therefore if the debt toward God presses, one must deprive the other. Hear him saying: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may have leisure for prayer and be together again—as if prayer sent up is not pure even for those who have come together, even if they have come together lawfully. One must also abstain from a woman in the time of her period, and it is counted a great charge to come together with a woman who is in her period. In Ezekiel’s catalog of brave deeds and of sins it is written that he will not approach a woman in her separation (Ezekiel 18:6). And one must be wholly pure also from one’s own wife in a time of prayer and fasting.

And again, he says, be together, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. This I say by way of concession, not of command (1 Corinthians 7:5–6). Everywhere he loosens the word because of weakness, and again tightens it to turn the hearers. I wish all people to be as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that (1 Corinthians 7:7). Marriage breathes of gift when the measures are kept—those of agreement. And one can truly say of some that for this one marriage is a gift, when there is no disorder, when there is all peace, all agreement. Yet to say that marriage of a believer with a Gentile woman, or of a Gentile with a believing woman, is a gift from God—this I would not say. For the gift of God cannot reach the Gentiles; if she believes, if she is saved, then she will begin to receive the gift.

title: Against Marcion; widows, remarriage, and unequally yoked (1 Cor 7)
english: Those from Marcion also use this saying, and without sense they forbid marriage, saying that chastity is a command of the other god whom they invented beside the Creator. Yet from the saying itself one can prove to them that they forbid marriage badly, and badly divide the Godhead. For if there is a gift to one in this way and to another in that, marriage also is a gift; if marriage is a gift, marriage the gift is badly forbidden; if the one in this way and the other in that are from God, it is clear that one God is the giver of chastity and the giver of marriage, and one is the God of the law and of the gospel, whom the prophets first proclaimed and later Christ Jesus.

But I say to the unmarried and to the widows that it is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they are not practicing self-control, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn. To the married I give charge—not I but the Lord—that a wife not be separated from a husband—but if she is separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to the husband—and that a husband not send away a wife. To the rest I say, I not the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:8–12).

Some among us teach beyond what is written; and thinking they are doing something, when they ought to exhort to single marriage without laying a snare on those who cannot, they do not do this, but impose necessity and wish not to gather the twice-married nor to share with them as with those who have transgressed, not respecting even the apostle’s voices. For the one who says to the unmarried and the widows, if they are not continent let them marry, openly permitted after the first marriage, after a woman has been widowed, to marry—while blaming the one who marries and the one who is married; for he said: If they are not continent, let them marry. See whether not being continent is not already an accusation—as when it is said to Christian people: Better to marry than to burn—he naming as burning the desire of the flesh not quenched by the Word but mastering the sinner’s soul. We therefore, taught by the apostle, do not forbid remarriage; for by comparison with burning, remarriage is more choiceworthy. Yet when something is thought better by comparison with evils, that thing is clearly not good. The second marriage is not temperance; it is not according to the nature of Adam the first-formed; for one cannot say to the second wife: This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh (Genesis 2:23). Abraham had also Hagar, and came to be also with Keturah; yet when he died, none was laid with him except the wife by nature; for Abraham and Sarah were in the tomb. And Jacob too, even if he had been with Rachel and with Leah and also with the maidservants, yet in the tomb only Leah was with him. With the mystical economy of the fathers; yet surely even now the one who takes a second does not say: I am fulfilling a mystical economy. For Paul will come saying: Tell me, you who read the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written: So-and-so had two sons, and so on; it will not also be said over him: These things are allegorized, for these women are two covenants; for these things happened typically to them, but were written for us upon whom the ends of the ages have come (Galatians 4:21–24; 1 Corinthians 10:11).

I say to the widows and to the unmarried that it is good for them if they remain as I also am. This is a second good; for there is another good first before this: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. What second good? It is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they are not continent, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn. Therefore those in first marriages who have not yet experienced second ones should practice chastity, that if something human happens they may not, caught untrained, behave shamefully. Better, then, to marry a second marriage—for he does not mean the first here, as is clear from the wording “to burn.” From here he passes to another legislation: To the married I give charge, not I but the Lord; the legislation toward the married is not from me but from the Lord. At the same time he keeps a necessary observation: he named “married” when both are believers, both the husband and the wife. That he did not name among the married the others who are unequally yoked is clear from his adding: To the rest I say, I not the Lord. Are the rest then not married? title: Lord’s charge, holiness in mixed marriage, circumcision paradigm (1 Cor 7)
english: of prayers and of holy childbearing and of all things in which Christians must share, he says that marriage is not alien to God. I charge, then—not I but the Lord—that a wife not be separated from a husband. The primary point is this: a yoking that has already been bound must not be loosed. But if she is also separated—for many causes of separation can arise; for example if fornication happens to the wife, it is a sin to keep the wife who has fornicated. If then she is also separated and some cause of separation arises, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to the husband. Likewise I also want a husband to be such that he not send away a wife. To the rest I say, I not the Lord. To those who have married I do not legislate, but the Lord; to those not married but unequally yoked with unbelievers I do not have a law to give from God; for they are not even worthy of God’s laws; but let them hear us. And I will use what is written in the law to make the matters of the place understood. The laws according to Moses—some are God’s, and some are Moses’. And knowing this difference of God’s laws and Moses’ laws, the Lord said concerning those legislated by God: For God said, Honor father and mother; and concerning those by Moses: Moses, because of your hardness of heart, allowed you to dismiss your wives (Matthew 19:8). If you keep the matters of the book of divorce you will find the law written not from a command of the Lord. Moses then, serving God, gave second laws beside the laws of God; Paul, serving the gospel, gave second laws to those of the church after the laws from God through Jesus Christ. And it is good to hear laws from the Lord rather than to hear laws of Paul the apostle. For even if he is holy, still he has laws far lesser than the laws of the Lord.

For the unbelieving husband is made holy in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy in the brother (1 Corinthians 7:14). As a kind of blending happens of the two, husband and wife, into one flesh, as of wine and water; and as the believer imparts holiness to the Gentile spouse, or the reverse—the believing woman to the unbelieving husband—so also the unbeliever imparts pollution to the believing wife, or the unbelieving wife to the believing husband. Why then does he say the unbeliever is made holy by receiving something from the believer, and is not also profaned by receiving something from the unbelieving part? For each, conversing from the abundance of the heart with the other, either imparts or receives, and in time the one entirely conquers the other. And what need, he says, of such a contest and danger? For either he will succeed or fail, and either he will lose his soul as well or, after much toil, scarcely be able to gain. Therefore it is good, before a person is forestalled, carefully to look not only at this but also at what is coming, and having looked either not to marry or, marrying, to marry in the Lord. For a wife is bound as long as her husband lives; but if the husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39). We do not hear the “only in the Lord,” but we read “she is free to be married to whom she wishes,” and we no longer set beside it “only in the Lord.” And yet even there, when he said “only in the Lord,” he again checked the word saying she is more blessed if she remains so, according to my judgment. So the apostle, having said the more auspicious thing—“For she is made holy”—left us to understand the other.

Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping God’s commandments. Let each remain in the calling in which he was called (1 Corinthians 7:18–20). It will seem that he has unseasonably cast beside the word about marriage and chastity, since no inquiry had arisen about those from circumcision who believe not needing to draw the foreskin, and again those in uncircumcision not needing to be circumcised, and about “Were you called a slave? title: Celibacy and marriage as indifferent; remain in your calling (1 Cor 7)
english: this also here he names a slave the one called after marriage, and free the unmarried. What is said about circumcision and about slaves is therefore said with a view to the place. Yet it is not out of place sometimes to use the saying against those who think after the faith one must be circumcised from a reverence—yet a reverence not according to knowledge—because of what is written in the old covenant about circumcision. Again it is not good, because of certain ones from circumcision who believe and think circumcision brings them shame and wish to draw a foreskin, to use the saying that says: Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. And there is reason to say to such that in itself circumcision is a matter of indifference. So now it is neither about circumcision nor about uncircumcision, but about the unmarried and the married: Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised—as if he were saying: Let him not draw a wife; he has already been circumcised; he put away a wife; let him not marry another. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised—as if: You were called in marriage; do not put away your wife. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing. Since some think the unmarried has something more in this respect than the married, and the married something less than the unmarried by the very fact of having married, we wish, he says, to teach that in its own account celibacy is indifferent and in its own account marriage is indifferent. For the one who is unmarried and truly pure from every mixture, yet living badly in other ways, may gain no benefit from celibacy; and someone in marriage, doing the things of marriage in order and season, keeping the rest of the way of life, may be no less than the unmarried. That celibacy itself and purity itself are indifferent we will prove thus. If only those from the church practiced celibacy, one might say that celibacy in its own account is something pure and divine; but now one can find also those unmarried with a base intention. Those from Marcion also practice celibacy and purity, but not as the church’s people do; for these do so to please the God who created the world, those so as not to cooperate with the god of the world. Celibacy is adorned by an ecclesiastical life and word, by pure knowledge and truth. So also the unmarried is indifferent in his own account; and it is possible also for one in marriage to be without blame, as we have already given. Circumcision then is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, both according to the wording and according to what is set before us. But what is it that saves? Keeping God’s commandments. For everyone who looses one of these least commandments and teaches people so—he did not say will not enter the kingdom of the heavens but will be called least in the kingdom of the heavens (Matthew 5:19). And if the one who loosed one of the least commandments will be called least in the kingdom of the heavens, where will the one who loosed two commandments be found? Let each therefore remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called in marriage? Do not envy the unmarried. Were you called unmarried? Do not by all means draw a foreskin, if you are able to live more purely.

Were you called a slave? Do not be concerned about it; but if you are also able to become free, rather use it. For the one called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise the one called free is Christ’s slave. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Brothers, let each remain with God in that in which he was called (1 Corinthians 7:21–24). title: Freedman in the Lord; virginity beyond command (1 Cor 7)
english: called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; as if: Were you called a slave? Know this, that you are not only not a slave, but you also have something of freedom because of the Lord. For the freedman is neither purely free nor still a slave, so that the one wholly pure is free and the one in marriage a slave; but when he is a slave in the Lord, then we say he is the Lord's freedman. And the one called free is a slave not of a wife but of the Word of God. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings. With all your strength understand the one who bought us out, the Word of God; let us propitiate the blood poured out for us. We were saying in the word about unmarried and married that he tightens and loosens the word. So also here he has done, saying: Do not become slaves of human beings; for he as it were tightens and makes the word sharper, exhorting those able, as far as possible, to live purely, and each to live purely in the calling in which he was called. And one must know that the other interpreters have given the sense about uncircumcision and circumcision according to the letter; for customarily, they say, he passes from what is before him to other things, legislating for all what is fitting.

Now concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give an opinion as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy (1 Corinthians 7:25). Of the commandments some are commanded, and some are not commanded but left free and entrusted to choice by God. For those without which one cannot be saved—these are the ones commanded; but the greater ones than the commanded, which even if we do not do we are saved, are not a command of God. Hear, he says, the gospel of Jesus Christ teaching in it and saying: when you have done all that is commanded you, you ought to say we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do (Luke 17:10). And if, when I do all that is commanded, I am an unprofitable servant, when will I flee being an unprofitable servant? If being more ambitious you ascend from what is commanded; for example: if I keep "you shall not commit adultery" and not looking at a woman to desire her, I have done what I ought. But if I remain a virgin, not ordered and not commanded, I no longer say over the achievement of virginity: we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought. So also on the remaining commandments: if I do not steal or overreach, we ought to say we are unprofitable servants. But if I sell all that I have and give to the poor, I no longer say I am unprofitable; I have done what I ought. Therefore the apostle says: Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give an opinion as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy. For in the Lord's saying to the disciples not all receive the word but those to whom it has been given, and he adds: let the one who is able to receive it receive it (Matthew 19:11–12); he did not command, but left it free. So I give an opinion, says the apostle, and to show that the Lord speaks in him he said as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy.

I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity, that it is good for a person to be thus (1 Corinthians 7:26). By necessity he means the sojourn in the body, as also elsewhere he says: but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake (Philippians 1:24). Four times in the place the apostle named the good; for he says first: it is good for a man not to touch a woman; second: it is good for them if they remain as I also am; third: I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity; fourth: it is good for a person to be thus. You see how many things said about chastity are named with the good; but whatever is said about marriage, with the marrying person's not sinning.

Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be loosed. Are you loosed from a wife? Do not seek a wife (1 Corinthians 7:27). Through the whole discourse, as has been said, he tightens and loosens, that the hearer, taking it in his own authority, may judge what he is able and to what exercise he can give himself. So also here he turned away from loosing marriage, and again exhorts to live purely. Therefore he called the married husband bound; and if to be bound is a circumstance, one must flee circumstances as far as possible. And do not seek to loose being bound to a wife; and the one not bound ought to guard himself lest he be bound; for truly you will find them bound by the marital love-charm. It is not permitted, then, for the one forestalled in marriage to seek untimely freedom, but to remain in the slavery; and if someone has been loosed, not to seek a wife. title: Fleshly affliction; soldier, farmer, shepherd and unused right (1 Cor 7–9)
english: if the virgin also marries, she has not sinned; again he did not say "good," but "she has not sinned." But such will have affliction in the flesh (1 Corinthians 7:28). For how will they not have affliction when what was said to the woman comes upon the married woman: In pain you will bear children, and your turning will be toward your husband, and he will rule over you (Genesis 3:16)? From all these the virgin is free, set free by purity, awaiting a bridegroom of blessing. Every marriage happens in darkness; therefore not in beds and wantonness (Romans 13:13). But Christ's marriage, when he receives his church, happens in the light. Why then do virgins enter the wedding with lamps and oil that lasts? Because that marriage is of seemliness. The one joined to flesh is one body; but the one joined to spirit is one spirit (1 Corinthians 6:16–17). And what is more seemly than a soul joined to spirit and united with it, no longer being a soul but becoming what the spirit is? For of marriage it was said: the two will become one flesh; but of the one joined to the Lord: he will be one spirit.

Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who shepherds a flock and does not eat of the milk of the flock? Do I say these things according to a human way? Or does not the law also say these things? For in the law of Moses it is written: You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing (1 Corinthians 9:7–9). As a God-fearing soldier the apostle says: Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? As one entrusted with God's field and farming the church: Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? As a disciple of the good shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep: Who shepherds a flock and does not eat of the milk of the flock? And as a soldier he also teaches us to serve, saying: No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please the one who enlisted him (2 Timothy 2:4); as a farmer he also teaches us to farm: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). And about shepherds the prophets taught us, recounting the wages of the good and announcing the punishments of those who shepherd otherwise. And the apostle will seem to one not attending to the Scripture to have forgotten what is before him through these things; but the truth is not so—he holds to the word. It is before him to teach about food offered to idols, that even if someone professing knowledge says he is not harmed by using idol-food, yet if he becomes a cause of harm to others, he ought to have cared for his neighbor, lest on his pretext others be destroyed. For this he takes the examples and says: Not in every case, if we have authority over something, ought we to make full use of the authority. For whether he is a soldier, he does not serve so as to secure nothing for himself from the rations; or a farmer, he is not content with the wage but eats from the grape; or a shepherd, besides the wage he shares the milk. So also I ought, besides the promises laid up for me from having served or farmed or shepherded well, to share in this world the things needed from those under me as soldiers, those farmed, those shepherded. Yet even if I have authority over the things needed, looking to the building up of people I do not make full use of the authority, in awe of giving some cutting-off to the gospel of Christ, or of giving a pretext to those who walk disorderly and work nothing but are busybodies (2 Thessalonians 3:11). Just as I do not use the authority I received from the Word, in the same way you also who claim to be wise ought not to use the authority but to provide for the building up of neighbors. And if the word seems to some to be without witness and spoken by human reasoning, let him hear the law saying: You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing, and what follows.

Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Or does he speak entirely for our sake? For it was written for our sake, that the one plowing ought to plow in hope and the one threshing to share in hope. title: Plowing in hope; necessity vs choice; all things to all (1 Cor 9)
english: the divine Jeremiah who says to them: Break up your fallow ground, clearly for the reception of seeds, about which it is written: The sower went out to sow (Jeremiah 4:3; Matthew 13:3). And after sowing the newly broken ground he says: I watch the seeds, lest the birds of the heaven come and take the seed; and when it bears fruit and makes fruits of righteousness and when it is already white toward harvest, it is then permitted me to take. For he will not be scandalized when he remembers how much I have toiled that I may plow his soul, that I may sow, how I persisted up to the point his seed came finished to the threshing floor. And for this reason it is permitted me to take foods from him. But I have not by all means used the authority; yet I do this in hope, to present the produce to the master of the house; for I am a farmer; not that I may take into my own storehouses the things owed to be rendered to God. Then teaching something about the same the apostle says: If we sowed spiritual things for you, is it a great thing… and what follows.

For if I proclaim the gospel, it is no ground for me to boast; for necessity is laid upon me; and woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship (1 Corinthians 9:16–17). We are taught that whatever we do from necessity has no boast; but whatever we do by choice, with no necessity laid on, these things have a boast. For example: the one who does not commit adultery or murder does not have a boast, but the one who lives as a virgin; for he did not come to virginity from necessity but from choice. And where "woe" stands beside if I do not do it, I have no boast. Therefore he says: If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship. Again we are taught something catholic. Some things we do willingly with the whole soul; some things we do, yet not willingly nor with the whole soul, but from grief or from necessity. Of the things done by us willingly there is a reward; of the things done, yet as from grief, there is neither reward nor punishment. For example: I give alms; if willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I am not charged with those who hear: I was hungry and you did not give me to eat, and what follows (Matthew 25:42). This then is the reward: that where I have authority I may not do it.

For though I am free from all, I enslaved myself to all, that I might gain the more; and I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain Jews; to those under the law as under the law—though not myself under the law—that I might gain those under the law; to those without law as without law—not being without law toward God but under Christ's law—that I might gain those without law; I became to the weak as weak, that I might gain the weak; I have become all things to all, that by all means I might save some. And I do all things for the sake of the gospel, that I may become a fellow-sharer in it (1 Corinthians 9:19–23). To be free from all is of a perfect apostle. For someone can be free from fornication but a slave of anger, free from love of money but a slave of empty glory; he can be free from one sin but a slave of another. But to say "being free from all" is of a perfect apostle—such as Paul was. And according to what is before us the sense is such: I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain Jews—for being free from Judaism I enslaved myself to Jews, that I might gain Jews; being free from being under the law I made myself as under the law, that I might gain those under the law. For Paul would go down into synagogues of Jews, would go in to them, would do according to their customs without harm, not sharing their pretense but hunting some from them. Some have asked what the difference is of those under the law beside the Jews; we say then that those under the law are other than Jews, as Samaritans. To those without law as without law: he came to Athens; he found philosophers there; he used not prophetic words nor legal ones, but wherever there was a lesson from Greek preparatory education he, recalling it, spoke to Athenians; for he says: as also some of your own poets have said, for we too are his offspring (Acts 17:28). There to those without law he became as without law, that he might gain those without law. And again he says: going through and observing your objects of worship, I found also an altar on which was inscribed: To an unknown god. What therefore you worship in ignorance, this I proclaim to you (Acts 17:23). And through these he begins to hand on reverence for God.
